etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English createn, from Latin creātus, the perfect passive participle of creō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). In this sense, mostly displaced Old English wyrċan (whence Modern English work) and ġesċieppan (whence Modern English shape).

definitions.definition: (especially of a god) To bring into existence out of nothing, without the prior existence of the materials or elements used.

quote.citation: 1560, [William Whittingham et al., transl.], The Bible and Holy Scriptures Conteyned in the Olde and Newe Testament. […] (the Geneva Bible), Geneva:  […]  Rouland Hall, →OCLC, Genesis I:1, folio 1, recto:
quote.text: In the beginning God created ye heauen and the earth. And the earth was without forme & voyde, and darkenes was vpon the depe, & the Spirit of God moued vpon the waters.

definitions.definition: To make or produce from other (e.g. raw, unrefined or scattered) materials or combinable elements or ideas; to design or invest with a new form, shape, function, etc.

quote.citation: 2013 June 8, “The new masters and commanders”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8839, page 52:
quote.text: From the ground, Colombo’s port does not look like much. […]  But viewed from high up in one of the growing number of skyscrapers in Sri Lanka’s capital, it is clear that something extraordinary is happening: China is creating a shipping hub just 200 miles from India’s southern tip.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To bring into existence; (sometimes in particular:)

quote.citation: 1829, Thomas Tully Crybbace, An Essay on Moral Freedom:
quote.text: [...] God created man a moral agent.

quote.citation: 2012 March-April, Terrence J. Sejnowski, “Well-connected Brains”, in American Scientist, volume 100, number 2, page 171:
quote.text: Creating a complete map of the human connectome would therefore be a monumental milestone but not the end of the journey to understanding how our brains work.

quote.citation: 2013 June 21, Oliver Burkeman, “The tao of tech”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 2, page 48:
quote.text: The dirty secret of the internet is that all this distraction and interruption is immensely profitable. Web companies like to boast about "creating compelling content",  […]  "share the things you love with the world" and so on. But the real way to build a successful online business is to be better than your rivals at undermining people's control of their own attention.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause, to bring (a non-object) about by an action, behavior, or event, to occasion.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter VII, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: The turmoil went on—no rest, no peace.  […]  It was nearly eleven o'clock now, and he strolled out again. In the little fair created by the costers' barrows the evening only seemed beginning; and the naphtha flares made one's eyes ache, the men's voices grated harshly, and the girls' faces saddened one.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To confer or invest with a rank or title of nobility, to appoint, ordain or constitute.

quote.citation: c. 1587–1588, [Christopher Marlowe], Tamburlaine the Great.  […]  The First Part […], 2nd edition, part 1, London:  […]  [R. Robinson for] Richard Iones, […], published 1592, →OCLC; reprinted as Tamburlaine the Great (A Scolar Press Facsimile), Menston, Yorkshire, London: Scolar Press, 1973, →ISBN, Act I, scene i:
quote.text: Create him Prorex of Affrica,That he may win the Babilonians hearts,Which will reuolt from Perſean gouernment,Unleſſe they haue a wiſer King than you.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be or do something creative, imaginative, originative.
(transitive) In theatre, to be the first performer of a role; to originate a character.
(UK, intransitive, colloquial) To make a fuss, complain; to shout.

quote.citation: 1972, H. E. Bates, The Song of the Wren:
quote.text: 'What's the time?' she said. 'I must fly. Miss'll start creating.'

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: Hearts create of duty and zeal.

quote.citation: 1814, Dante Alighieri, “Canto III”, in H[enry] F[rancis] Cary, transl., The Vision; or, Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise, of Dante Alighieri. […], volume I (Hell), London:  […]  [J. Barfield] for Taylor and Hessey, […], →OCLC, page 10, lines 7–9:
quote.text: Before me things create were none, save things / Eternal, and eternal I endure. / All hope abandon ye who enter here. [Inscription on the gate of Hell.]
